p.
1) Oṃ, homage to the embodiment of auspiciousness!
Now,
The Heart of Recognition. Salutation to Śiva, who eternally performs the fivefold cosmic act, and who illumines the ultimate reality of one’s own self, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss. (1)

From the great ocean of the *Pratyabhijñā*, which is the essence of the *Śāṅkara Upaniṣads*, the quintessence is extracted by Kṣema for the sake of pacifying the poison of transmigratory existence. (2) [In some versions, the reading is:
"I extract the supreme essence, which bestows the pacification of the poison of transmigratory existence."]

In this context, there are those of delicate intellect who have not undergone the labor of studying the treatises on sharp reasoning, yet whose desire for immersion (*samāveśa*) has been awakened by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and who, through the force of that descent of power, long for the supreme lordly state.

[The reading: Some are devoted to them; for their essence of the instruction on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*—since consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action are therein most clearly manifest—is as follows:
[tattvaṃ hi cidānandaiṣaṇājñānakriyāṇāṃ susphuṭatvataḥ].
The pentad of principles known as Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśāna, and Vidyā.
Thus it is handed down as a group of five. The meaning of the sentence is that "it is opened" means it is revealed in an abbreviated form for their sake. [p. 2] It is opened slightly.

In this regard, he says [the following] in order to manifest that one's own self-deity alone is the cause everywhere, is attainable through easy means, and yields great fruit. (Note: *kh* and *ṅ* do not contain the word "sarvatra"; *k* and *g* read "and he speaks of the manifestation of the great fruit.")
Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe. || 1 ||

The Blessed Lady, who is consciousness in the form of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), is indeed the one who effects the accomplishment, manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal—characterized by resting within the supreme subject—of the entire universe, from Sadāśiva down to the earth. [Note: In the *kha* and *ṅga* manuscripts, the reading is "sve cetyātmani" (within her own nature of the object of thought).]

The independent [power], consisting of the supreme *vimarśa*—[in the manuscript *kh* and *ṅ*, the reading is *tantrānantavimarśamayī*]—which is non-different from the venerable Lord Śiva, is the cause—the instrument. For when this [power] unfolds, the universe emerges and persists; and when its unfolding has ceased, [the universe likewise withdraws]. *kh*, *ṅ*...
The word "ca" (and) is not present in the text. Regarding the phrase "it blinks," one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*) alone is the witness here.
As for anything else—such as *māyā* or *prakṛti*, which is distinct from the light of consciousness—it is non-existent because it does not manifest;
therefore, it can never function as a cause. [In the manuscript *kh*, the reading is "aprakāśatvena" (by way of non-manifestation); in *ṅ*, it is "asattvād api" (even because of non-existence).]

[The reading is "na kvacit hetutvam" (there is no causality anywhere). However, in the case of being manifest, because it is identical with manifestation, consciousness (*cit*) itself, whose nature is manifestation, is the cause. (p. 3) [The reading in manuscripts *kh* and *ṅ* is "cideva" (consciousness alone).]
But it is not something else at all; for this very reason, distinctions of place, time, and form are not applicable to consciousness, as it has been said:
"A distinction of place, time, and form is not possible for consciousness."

"Therefore, consciousness alone is said to be the one, perfect *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (the reflective awareness of 'I'). Created by this and animated by this—[in the manuscripts *k* and *g*, the reading is *etat-prāṇitāḥ*]—nothing is capable of breaking its essential nature; thus, it is of a pervasive, eternally risen, and perfectly full form. This... [manuscript *k*: ...]

"This is complete"; [in the *g* manuscript, the reading is "this is complete" (*paripūrṇeyam*)]. This is indeed obtained through the sense of the text [in the *k*, *g*, and *ṅ* manuscripts, the reading is "this is obtained without effort" (*ity ayatnalabhyam eva*)].
Now, one might object: the world is not at all distinct from consciousness; and if there is no distinction, how can there be the relationship of cause and effect?

[Regarding the reading "How is there the existence of the cause? It is said: The Blessed Lady, Consciousness itself, whose nature is pure and autonomous, flashes forth as the self of each and every infinite world—in this universal form (*viśvarūpa*). This alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

The relationship of cause and effect: since this very [consciousness] is the cause for the establishment— that is, the manifestation— of the universe consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, therefore, of this [consciousness], which is independent, unlimited, and self-luminous by nature...
When established, it consists in the manifestation of a novel object (*abhinavārthaprakāśanarūpa*). (p. 4) [In the manuscript *kh*, the reading is *svatantrāvicchinnā*; in *g*, it is *siddhau*.]

Regarding "the manifestation of a new object" (*abhinavārthaprakāśana*); [the reading is *abhinavaprakāśarūpam*]. A wretched means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is neither employed nor appropriate [for this], because another lamp is not required for the illumination of the sun—this is the sense. As it has been said in the *Trikasāra*:

Just as one who desires to step over the shadow of his own head finds that the head cannot exist at the place where the foot is, so too it is with this *baindavī* digit; the connection here is: "for him who desires to step over it, just as the head would not be at the location of the foot, so it is with this."
Thus,

because she is the cause of the manifestation of the universe and of its withdrawal— which consists in the attainment of the state of non-dual equilibrium with the Supreme— she is therefore autonomous (*svatantrā*).
"Having realized her own sovereignty, she is the cause of all the accomplishments of the universe, which consist of both enjoyment and liberation"— this is to be explained by repeating the phrase.

Moreover, the universe— consisting of the blue, pleasure, the body, the vital breaths, and so forth [the blue being accessible through the external senses, pleasure through the internal sense, and the vital breaths through the activity of the living being]—
is that which is established by means of the sequential process of ascending through the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus; [g: the reading is *pramāṇopāharaṇakrameṇa*] immersion into the subject consisting of reflective awareness [kh:

the reading is *vimarśamātrāveśa*]; that very [state] is the cause [as the meaning is: just as smoke is the means for the inference of a distant fire, so it is]. [kh, ṅ: that very thing] is the cause.
The reading is *hetuḥ*—that which has [this] as its means for thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*).
By this, its nature as an easy means (*sukhopāyatva*) is stated. As it is said in the *Śrī-Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
The cognition of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings;
however, this is the distinction for yogins: their attentiveness toward that relationship.
Thus,
the singular form "citiḥ" (consciousness), by expressing its state of being unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, [according to the reading:
"expresses precisely its non-conditioned state"] indicates the unreality of all doctrines that maintain duality.

It reveals: the word "independent" (*svatantra*), expressing its distinction from the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*), declares that consciousness has sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) as its essence. The phrase beginning with "the universe" (*viśva*) expresses the state of possessing all powers (*aśeṣaśaktitva*).
[The reading is "possessing all powers" (aśeṣaśaktimattvam)]. This states that it is the cause of everything, that its means are easy, and that its fruit is great. || 1 ||

Now, one might object: "If consciousness (*citi*) is the cause of the universe, then, given its dependence on material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth, the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*) would not be abandoned. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By her own will, she unfolds the universe upon her own screen..."
He dissolves. || 2 ||
[He acts] by his own will, and not by the will of another like Brahmā and others;
and by that very [will], and not in dependence on material causes and so forth— thus.

For, due to the previously mentioned loss of autonomy, consciousness itself (*cittattva*) would not even be possible; it is not elsewhere that the universe, as previously determined, appears— like a city in a mirror—
as distinct, though non-distinct, upon its own wall.

"It opens up" (*unmīlayati*). And "opening up" (*unmīlanam*) is the manifestation of that which already exists—[note: after "unmīlayati," there is also an additional reading *avabhāsayati*]. By this, it is stated that the world abides in identity with light alone. (2)
Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of the universe through its divisions, he says:
"That [universe] is manifold due to the distinction between the corresponding object and subject. (3)
That universe is manifold, consisting of many diverse modes. How so?

It consists of objects of perception (*grāhya*) and subjects of perception (*grāhaka*)—the latter being the seven perceivers, among whom Śiva is the first—situated in mutual suitability (*anurūpa*), that is, established in mutual fitness. (Note: Regarding the variant reading *anaṇurūpāṇām* found in manuscript *kh*, it would mean "not of minute form," but the context here favors *anurūpāṇām*, which refers to the correspondence between subject and object.)

(2) the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśvaras), (3) the Lords of Mantra (mantreśvaras), (4) the Mantras, (5) the Vijñānākala, (6) the Pralayākala, and (7) the Sakala— these are well-known from the scriptures— and because of the distinction [of the subjectivity] (grāhakatābheda).

In the principle of Sadāśiva, the universe exists in a form that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāpara), consisting of an indistinct sense of "this-ness" (idantā) veiled by the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā). [Note: In manuscript k, the reading is *ahantācchādite 'pi sphuṭe idantāmayaṃ*.]

The object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is likewise the class of subjects known as the Great Lords of Mantra (*mantramaheśvara*), presided over by the venerable Lord Sadāśiva; their existence in that state is fashioned by the will of the Supreme Lord within the *Īśvara-tattva*.

Just as the universe to be grasped consists of the identity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "this-ness" and "I-ness," so too is the group of Mantreśvaras presided over by the Lord Īśvara-bhaṭṭāraka in the stage of *vidyā* (the *vidyā-tattva*).
Thus; [in the reading *vidyāpadeśa-śrīmat*, the text is as follows:
presided over by the venerable Lord Ananta, it is divided into many branches and intermediate subdivisions. [In manuscript G:
"presided over by the infinite and many-branched"; in K: "many-branched and divided into intermediate [sections]"; in Kh: ...]

[The reading is *adhiṣṭhitabahuśākha*. Just as the mantras and the subjects (*pramātṛ*) are of such a nature, so too is the universe—the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—whose sole essence is duality. Above Māyā, there are the Vijñānākalas, whose nature consists of pure consciousness devoid of agency (*kartṛtā*). [In manuscript *kh*, it reads "devoid of agency" (*kartṛtvaśūnya*).]

Their object of knowledge (*prameya*) is precisely that which consists of non-difference (*tad-abheda-sāra*), familiar from their prior state as *sakala* and *pralayākala*, within Māyā, for the subjects who are the void (*śūnya-pramātṛ*). [In the reading of manuscript k: "within Māyā..."]

[The reading is *pramātṛṇām*]. For the *pralayakevalins*, their own consciousness (*svacitta*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), being as if dissolved (*pralīnakalpa*). For those situated up to the level of the earth (*kṣitiparyanta*), [the reading is *sthitiparyanta* in manuscript *k*].

In the *Pāṭha*, however, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for all [limited subjects], who are entirely distinct and finite, is precisely of that same nature [as they perceive it]. For the venerable Lord Śiva, who transcends those [objects] and whose body is pure light, all entities are of the very nature of light alone. Furthermore, for the illustrious Paramaśiva, who is both transcendent of the universe and identical with the universe—
Or rather, it is the venerable Lord Paramaśiva himself who manifests in this way through thousands of diverse varieties;
thus, it has been essentially stated. (3)
And just as the Blessed One has a universal body (*viśvaśarīra*), so too does consciousness, though consisting of the contraction of *cit*, possess sentience.
He consists of the entire universe, yet remains contracted within himself.
The venerable Supreme Śiva, desiring to manifest the universe— which exists in identity with his own self— in the form appropriate to Sadāśiva and the others, first...
9) It manifests as the nature of the "void beyond the void" (*śūnyātiśūnya*), which is a synonym for Anāśrita Śiva, consisting of the non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) of the identity with consciousness;
it shines forth through its non-difference from the Light (*prakāśa*). From that [it proceeds].
He also manifests as the nature of all principles and worlds— which are the solidified form of the essence of consciousness— as well as in the form of various subjects and so forth.
Just as the Lord is thus the body of the universe, so too is he the contracted form of consciousness, whose nature consists in the contraction of consciousness.

[Regarding the reading *asaṃkucita*: ] The conscious perceiver (*cetana-grāhaka*) is likewise contracted into the form of the entire universe, like the seed-pod of a banyan tree (*vaṭadhānikā*). Thus, there is a statement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*):
"The body (*vigraha*) and the embodied one (*vigrahin*)—indeed, he is the possessor of all bodies."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Triśiromata*:
"O Dear One, listen now to that body which consists of all the gods. [Note: The reading in manuscript *kh* is "kālastaccedānīm" (time, then listen now).]
Earth is proclaimed by its solidity, and water by its fluidity.
Having begun thus,
Triśirobhairava himself stands pervading the entire universe.
With this much of the text, he declares that the subject (*grāhaka*) is indeed composed of the contracted universe.
And this is the intended meaning here: even this subject is [of the nature of] light—
10) By means of both scriptural authority and reasoning, it is stated that Śiva alone, whose single form is the body of the universe, exists;
however, because his true nature is unmanifest due to his power of *māyā*, he appears as such.

[The reading is *māyāśaktyanabhivyaktā* (unmanifested by the power of *māyā*). It appears as if contracted; yet even this contraction, when investigated, consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), because it is manifested as one with consciousness (*cidaikātmyena*).
As it has been stated in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, in the investigation of the definitions of the factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the agent and the object: "Having come together..."

For if all causal factors (*kāraka*) were equally engaged in producing an action, what would be the meaning of "the most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) or "independence" (*svatantra*)? Thus, the entire body of grammar (*sārvapāriṣadaṃ vyākaraṇam*) would be contradicted. For this very reason, they assert that the operation of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that operation of the knower resides within the knower whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*).

Because it exists as identity (*tādātmya*), it is of the nature of consciousness (*bodhātmaka*). And thus, in this very context, the case-roles (*kāraka*) arise according to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*): for example, "Consciousness accomplishes the universe"; "having reached Consciousness, the universe comes to be"; "by means of Consciousness, the Lord creates the universe"; "from Consciousness the universe arises"; "the universe is a modification (*vikāra*) of Consciousness"; [and] "in Consciousness..."
"The universe exists"—thus it is; otherwise, nothing at all exists. Therefore, every subject is none other than the venerable Śiva, whose body is the universe.
As I have stated myself:
If non-manifestation does not manifest, then manifestation alone remains.
If it does manifest, then because its nature is that of manifestation, manifestation alone remains.
Thus, with this very intention, it is stated in the venerable Spandaśāstras (p.
"Because the individual soul consists of everything... [and so forth].
Having begun thus, he says:

"Therefore, in the investigations of word-meanings [kh, ṅ: *tasmācchabdārtha*]; g: the reading is *tasmātsarvārtha*]—that is, in other investigations of word-meanings such as 'he wishes to fall from the bank' (*taṭaḥ pipatiṣati*) and so forth..."
How could desire be possible for an insentient bank? There is no state that is not Śiva.

By these and other such statements, the non-difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) alone has been declared. That the thorough knowledge of this very reality is liberation, and the lack of thorough knowledge of this very reality is bondage—this will indeed come to pass. 4.

Now, one might object: "This subject consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptualization is caused by the mind (*citta*). Since the mind exists, how can this subject have the nature of Śiva? Having raised this doubt, [the author] speaks in order to determine the true nature of the mind:
"Consciousness (*cit*) itself, having descended from the state of pure sentience (*cetana*) into the state of the object of thought (*cetya*)..."
The mind is that which contracts [into the state of subject-object duality]. || 5 ||
That which is called "mind" (citta) is nothing other than that very same [consciousness]; indeed, it is the Blessed Lady herself. For she is her own essential nature.
When, having concealed it, one assumes contraction,
then there are two possible courses: sometimes, having subordinated even that which has arisen as contraction, [one proceeds].

It manifests sometimes with consciousness as predominant and sometimes with contraction as predominant. In the case where consciousness is predominant—that is, when there is predominance of innate pure luminosity—there is the state of a *vijñānākala*. However, when there is predominance of the reflective awareness of that luminosity, there is the subjectivity of *vidyā*. Even in that case:

When the contraction gradually becomes attenuated, there arises the nature of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita; however, when the state in which consciousness is predominant is attained through the effort of *samādhi*— [Note: The text provided in the prompt contains various manuscript variants, such as *saṃkocāṃśatanutāyām*, *saṃkocatanutāyām*, and *samādhiprayatnopārjitena*. The translation above reflects the most coherent reading based on the context of Trika/Kashmiri Śaiva philosophy.]
[The reading is *citpradhānatvena*] the state of being a subject on the pure path (*śuddhādhva*) becomes increasingly more excellent step by step.

However, when contraction (*saṃkoca*) predominates—as in the reading *saṃkocāṃśaprādhānyena*—there arises the state of subjects such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth. Such being the case, it remains exactly thus.
[The reading is *sati*]: Consciousness itself, having descended from the state of pure consciousness (*cetanapada*) into the form of a contracted grasper—
being oriented toward the apprehension of objects— is "existent" (*satī*) and becomes contracted by the object of cognition (*cetya*), such as blue, pleasure, and so forth.
The mind is indeed contracted by the contraction of both [subject and object]. And thus (p.
"The knowledge and the action of the Lord which exist toward entities that are of the nature of His own limbs..."
In the third state, which is Māyā, those same qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—belong to the bound soul (paśu).

By such statements as these, it is shown that the very power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), whose nature is autonomy (*svātantrya*), takes the form of the powers of knowledge, action, and *māyā* in the state of the bound soul (*paśu*) due to the intensity of contraction (*saṃkoca*). [Note: The reading *iti pratyabhijñoktanītyā svātantryeti pāṭhaḥ* is supported by the source; the variant *saṃkocaprakāśāt* found in manuscript *k* is noted. It is from this [autonomy] that the three qualities (*sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*) arise.

[The phrase "it is stated in the Śrīpratyabhijñā" does not exist in the text. For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrītattvagarbhastotra* that because the true nature exists even in the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one should act with the intention of following that [true nature]; [the reading in manuscript *kh* is *tadanusāriṇā*].
For this very reason, however, for those who follow the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
their own nature (*svarūpa*) therein— [g, ṅ: for them, even there, the nature...]— is [as follows].
Even in the state of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), its nature as self-luminous (*svajyotiṣṭva*) is not lost—this is the reading accompanied by a synonym.
Thus [ends the fifth].
But consciousness alone is the essential nature of the subject of illusion; thus he says: "The subject of illusion consists of that. (6)
To begin with, the state of body and breath is primarily that of the mind alone. (p. 14) [In the manuscript Ṅ, the reading is: "From the state of body and breath, the mind is primarily [the focus].

The ground (bhūmi) as well possesses mental formations (*cittasaṃskāra*); otherwise, for one who has emerged from that state, there would be no pursuit of their own duties. Thus, the illusory subject (*pramātā*) consists of nothing but consciousness (*cittamaya*).
With this very intention, in the *Śivasūtras*, in accordance with the actual nature of things... [g: ...]
[The reading is *vastuvṛttyanusāreṇa*.

Consciousness is the self (*ātman*). [Regarding the phrase "consciousness is the self": it is conscious (*cetana*) because it cognizes; it is independent in all cognitions and in all actions. Its state is consciousness (*caitanya*), which consists of the connection with all cognitions and actions.

Having stated in the first aphorism that "that perfect sovereignty belongs only to the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva and not to others who are dependent upon him," he further states in the third Unmeṣa: "The mind is the Self.
The meaning of this is as follows: because it is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects, this [mind] is eternally...

The mind (*citta*), which consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*), and the mental organ (*manas*)—characterized by functions such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth—is that very thing which "wanders" (*atati*);

because, through the non-manifestation of its own true nature consisting of consciousness (*cit*), it wanders among various wombs (*yonīḥ*) by relying on the fluctuations of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, it is therefore called the "Self" (*ātman*) and the "atomic" (*aṇu*). However, for this [Self] whose sole form is consciousness, there is no such wandering; for this very reason, it is said that "consciousness alone is the Self."

The Self was previously defined with the intention of demonstrating its essential nature as being its true, innate reality; however, by this [present definition], it is characterized according to its state as an impure *āṇava* subject, in which the manifestation of contraction is predominant. Thus, there is no inconsistency between what precedes and what follows. Having stated this, [the author] speaks again on the occasion of defining the subject (*pramātṛ*) of *māyā*.
It has been stated that "the mind is the self" (3-1). || 6 ||

Since liberation results from the correct knowledge of its very nature, whereas transmigratory existence results from incorrect [knowledge], he speaks in order to analyze this nature down to its smallest parts: (p. 15) [Note: the reading in manuscript G is *vibhaṅktum*].
And he is one, yet of two forms, consisting of three, having four natures, and possessing the essence of seven pentads. || 7 ||

From the perspective of definitive insight, the conscious self is none other than the venerable Śiva alone; it is the one Self and nothing else, because differentiation by means of space, time, and so forth is impossible for Light, whereas for that which is insentient, the status of being a subject is untenable.
For Light itself, by virtue of its sovereignty...

Having grasped the contraction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, it assumes the state of perceiving contracted objects; therefore, it is of two forms by virtue of being both of the nature of light and possessing the manifestation of contraction. The nature of the three impurities (*mala*) has been described by Āṇava [and Vāmadeva] as follows:
The contraction of this [Self], whose own greatness is concealed and who has forgotten its true nature due to delusion—that alone is called the individual (āṇava) impurity (mala). || 1 ||

The state of abiding in a body composed of the elements, resulting from the destruction of one's own natural condition through the pervasion of the six coverings (kañcukas), is called the impurity of Māyā.

That which, through the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the intellect (buddhi), the organs of action (karmendriya), and so forth, engages externally, is considered its "actional impurity" (kārma-mala). (3)

In that regard, one bound by the single impurity of *āṇava* is the *vijñānākala*; one bound by two—namely, being veiled by the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* impurities—is the *trimaya* (consisting of three);
and one bound by the three is the *śūnyākala*.
Because its nature is that of the body, it consists of four aspects. The seven pentads consist of the elements beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth.
[Note: In manuscript *k*, the reading "the pentads ending with Earth" appears without the word "beginning with Śiva."]

The thirty-five principles constitute its very nature. Likewise, although [the series] beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala consists of the forms of the powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, due to the power of non-recognition (akhyāti), they appear as limited by the kalās; yet, in reality, they are of the single nature of Śiva.

When recognized as consisting of the thirty-five principles (*tattva*), as being the nature of the seven subjects (*pramātṛ*), and as being composed of the five powers beginning with consciousness (*cit*), this [Self] bestows liberation; otherwise, however, it is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). || 7 ||
And thus, all three types of vision belong to that same level. || 8 ||

The established positions— the doctrines— of all schools of thought, such as the Cārvākas and others, are merely artificial roles assumed at will by this Self, like those of an actor. And so it is said:
"The self is the body qualified by consciousness," so say the Cārvākas. (p.

The Naiyāyikas and others consider the self in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti) to be essentially the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), which serves as the substratum for a multitude of qualities such as cognition; however, upon liberation (apavarga), they hold it to be almost non-existent once those qualities have been destroyed.
It is the object of the "I-notion" (ahaṃ-pratīti), conditioned by such adjuncts as pleasure and pain.
The reading begins with "pleasure and pain," etc. [Note: G and Kh read "the self is overcome by adventitious attributes such as suffering"].
Thinking that the self is thus obscured, the Mīmāṃsakas as well are settled upon nothing other than the intellect (buddhi).
The Buddhists conclude that reality is nothing but the continuum of cognition;
some knowers of the Upaniṣads maintain that the vital breath alone is the self.
"This was indeed non-existent"—thus do the proponents of Brahman as non-existence remain, having plunged into the realm of the void;
the Mādhyamikas likewise hold this same view.
